title: How a Nuclear Meltdown Works
summary: Special news-driven episode explaining how a nuclear meltdown works, prompted by the March 2011 Fukushima Daiichi crisis in Japan. The hosts cover catastrophe modeling and why plants were built for a 250-year quake, how a boiling water reactor produces steam power, control rods and scramming, decay heat, the loss of cooling after the tsunami knocked out pumps and diesel generators, hydrogen gas explosions and seawater flooding, the Mark I reactor design criticisms, comparisons to Three Mile Island and Chernobyl, radiation units (millisieverts and microsieverts), and iodine-131 and potassium iodide tablets. The episode closes with a listener mail about the Small Change Fund and a Canadian First Nations culture program, and asks listeners how to help Japan.

segments.title: Opening and framing the Japan crisis
segments.summary: Hosts introduce a special episode on nuclear meltdowns in response to the crisis in Japan, saying they will explain it in simple terms.

segments.title: Catastrophe modeling and plant earthquake design
segments.summary: Explanation of catastrophe risk modeling and how the Fukushima plants were built to withstand a 250-year earthquake, which they did, but the tsunami was not accounted for.

segments.title: How a nuclear plant makes power
segments.summary: Describes how a boiling water reactor uses uranium fission to boil water into steam that drives turbines, and how control rods modulate the reaction.

segments.title: Scramming, decay heat and loss of cooling
segments.summary: Explains scramming the reactor, why decay heat continues after shutdown, and how cooling pumps depend on electricity. The tsunami knocked out the grid, diesel generators, and then batteries ran only for a limited time.

segments.title: Hydrogen explosions and seawater flooding
segments.summary: Describes how exposed fuel overheated, hydrogen gas built up and exploded inside reactor buildings, and how operators flooded reactors with seawater. Explains that these were chemical explosions, not nuclear bombs.

segments.title: Meltdown risks, Mark I criticisms and Three Mile Island
segments.summary: Discusses the risk of fuel melting through containment, spent fuel fire at reactor four, the Mark I design criticized in 1972 and modifications made in the US, GE's role, and comparisons to Three Mile Island and Chernobyl.

segments.title: Radiation units and health risks
segments.summary: Explains millisieverts and sieverts, average annual radiation dose, and why radiation exposure is cumulative. Discusses how absorbed radioactive material is harmful.

segments.title: Iodine-131 and potassium iodide tablets
segments.summary: Explains iodine-131 as a radioactive byproduct that concentrates in the thyroid, and how taking iodide saturates the thyroid. Notes shortages and fake iodide warnings. Discusses the radioactive plume reaching the US and perspective about Denver.

segments.title: Radiation in Sacramento and perspective on everyday radiation
segments.summary: Reports small amounts of radioactive material detected in Sacramento that are not harmful, and notes radiation from granite at Grand Central Station and the US Capitol. Advises calm.

segments.title: How to help Japan
segments.summary: Hosts suggest donating to the Red Cross and sending help, and point listeners to an online overview of the crisis.

segments.title: Listener mail: Small Change Fund and Litchko Summer Culture Education Program
segments.summary: Listener Paul C from Canada asks the show to promote the Small Change Fund, which funds small startup projects, including a First Nations summer culture program.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to share ideas on social media and email, and close the episode.
